newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Headlines worry, but air safety trend positive.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Headlines worry, but air safety trend positive.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
If you plan to fly off on your holidays this Christmas or New Year; relax.
Forget the fact that airliner crashes have killed more people in the world this year than ever before.
According to aviation information consultancy Airclaims, 1,187 passengers have been killed in 1996, three times more than last year.

But despite this increase, described by aviation experts as a statistical blip, the overall trend is for an ever lower rate of accidents. Ballooning growth in travel may give the impression that the actual accident incidence is increasing.
PLANE CRASHES HOG HEADLINES, BUT CARS ARE SERIAL KILLERS

Spectacular catastrophes grab the headlines, like the mid-air collision between a Saudia Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Airlines Ilyushin IL-76 freighter near New Delhi last month, which killed 349.
But the carnage on the world's roads kills hundreds of thousands of people and goes largely unreported.

So while you're strapped in your seat at 37,000 feet, and the first sign of clear air turbulence starts to rattle the ice in your gin and tonic, don't worry. The cruising section of air travel almost never leads to accidents. It's the take-off and landing phase where most fatal accidents occur.

Drive from your mind thoughts of unsolved crashes involving the workhorse of world airlines, the Boeing 737. A USAir 737 dived from the sky approaching Pittsburgh in 1994, killing 132. A United Airlines 737 crashed in similar circumstances in Colorado Springs, Colorado in 1991 as did the so far unexplained TWA Boeing 747 crash off Long Island, New York last July which killed 230.
Experts say it is still much safer than travelling in a car, unless you are in an elderly jet, or flying into relatively dangerous airspace over continents like Africa.
LONG-TERM TREND IS FOR LESS ACCIDENTS

"I don't want to be complacent, but fortunately fatalities are relatively rare. Having an extra one or two crashes can make a considerable increase. The trend is to halve passenger deaths (per flight) every 10 years," said Airclaims director Paul Hayes.
Flight International Safety Editor David Learmount agrees.
"There are about 40 accidents every year including cargo planes. We've had about 34 so far this year, so in terms of numbers it's not been bad," Learmount said.

"But some have been very nasty this year. Since the previous worst year in 1985 (when 1,169 died in western built planes) there was only about half the amount of aviation that there is now; so this year is markedly safer than 1985."
DEVELOPING WORLD ACCOUNTS FOR BULK OF ACCIDENTS
Learmount said many of these accidents happen outside developed countries, where the car is more dangerous.

"Three quarters of the accidents happen in countries accounting for only 12 percent of overall world traffic. If you travel by car, the risk increases with distance. With the aeroplane it doesn't, practically nothing ever goes wrong in the cruise," Learmount said.
He said technological improvements in planes, in guidance systems and air traffic control are relentlessly improving safety standards.
OLDER JETS WORRY SOME EXPERTS

The bulk of the world's jet fleet still consists of Boeing 727 tri-jets, early 737s, McDonnell Douglas DC-9s and DC-10s, old 747s, Lockheed Tristars and early Airbuses. According to Learmount these old planes still present sound safety records. However later, highly automated 747s and Airbuses do have a better safety record, Learmount said, citing a Boeing study.
Some experts worry about hidden problems which might show themselves in older planes, which tend to migrate to less developed countries' airlines while western outfits buy new.
"Older jets are a serious concern to the industry. Reservations are expressed privately about the number of older aircraft," said Paul Beaver, spokesman for Jane's Defence Weekly.
The Trans World Airlines 747-100, lost off Long Island with 230 dead, was 27 years old, according to Beaver.

"Airlines don't know enough about them, or predict how they might react to certain problems. The first generation of aircraft like early 747s are nearly 30 years old. Discerning passengers only go where the equipment is new -- say less than 10 years old," Beaver said.
"It's not a crisis, just something they've got to be aware of."
AIR TRAVEL BOOM TO BE RELENTLESS

Whatever the real or perceived risk, the business of air travel is set to continue burgeoning. By 2014, the number of airliners in use will have doubled to about 18,000, according to John Westcott, chairman of Lloyd's Aviation Underwriters' Association.

"If by 2014 we have double the fleet and double the amount of take-offs and landings, without any improvement (in the accident rate) we would expect to have one airliner loss every week," Westcott said.
NOT START OF "EVIL TREND"
Westcott is confident that improvements were possible.
"The current position shows an improving long-term graph, but you do get glitches up and down," Westcott said.
Flight International's Learmount also believes the latest statistics represent a temporary aberation.

"This year the actual number of fatal accidents doesn't look much different from the average for 10 years, but the number killed is about double the number which was the average of the last 10 years."
"That will make a horrible spike in the graph, but you can bet your bottom dollar that it's a spike, not the start of some kind of evil trend," Learmount said.
HOW TO CURB THE HUMAN FACTOR?
Steadily improving technology will allow planes to find their way around the world more efficiently using satellites, avoid collisions, and take more work away from pilots.

The human factor is seen as the cause for most airliner accidents, and the International Air Transport Association has said it wants airlines to address this problem as part of its goal of cutting accidents by 50 per cent by 2004.
Would fully automated flight be the ultimate solution?
Experts doubt things will go that far in the forseeable future. One said he didn't think passengers would trust this, but saw some other possibilities.
"In the future the flight deck will consist of a pilot and a dog," he said. "The pilot will be there to monitor what's going on. The dog will make sure the pilot doesn't touch anything."
